                                      PROJECT NO. 58481


 RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                          §       PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                       §
 STANDARDS UNDER PURA §37.0561                    §                    OF TEXAS
                                                  §

 STACK INFRASTRUCTURE COMMENTS TO PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION IN
                       PROJECT NO. 58481



Introduction:

STACK Infrastructure (“STACK”) appreciates the opportunity to provide comments to the
proposal for publication in Project No. 58481. STACK is a proven, trusted partner for the
world’s most innovative companies, designing, developing, and operating sustainable global
digital infrastructure. Backed by an unmatched record of reliable delivery and development
expertise, STACK brings speed, scale, certainty, and responsibility to the demands of a rapidly
evolving digital infrastructure landscape.

Data center investment delivers significant economic and tax benefits to Texas and its local
communities but the magnitude of such investment requires a high degree of contractual and
regulatory certainty, particularly with respect to access to transmission service.

STACK supports the principle that large load customers, including data centers, should bear the
cost of transmission infrastructure required to serve them and should not shift those costs to other
rate classes. However, these financial commitments should also assign proportionate rights to the
large load customers. When a customer has funded or contractually committed to firm
transmission capacity, that capacity must remain available to that customer.

As drafted, §25.194(h) and similar capacity reallocation provisions in utility agreements allow
for the loss or reallocation of previously contracted transmission capacity, even after substantial
financial commitments have been made. This undermines the fundamental premise that
customers who pay for capacity should be able to rely on access to that capacity. The risk of
reallocation introduces material uncertainty that threatens investment and weakens Texas’
competitive position.

STACK supports the concept of Oncor’s position in Project 58484 advocating for capacity-
based, contractual rates that align cost responsibility with contracted capacity. The Commission
should consider this framework when finalizing the 58481 rule to ensure consistency between
cost responsibility and capacity rights.
 Accordingly, the Commission should eliminate and nullify capacity reallocation provisions for
new interconnections, including existing utility contracts executed prior to the effective date of
the rule, except in cases of clear and sustained non-performance against defined contractual
energization milestones.



Recommendation: Retain contracted transmission capacity.
Contracted transmission capacity should be retained by a large load customer throughout both
the load ramp and operational phases and should not be subject to reallocation absent clear,
sustained non-performance against defined contractual milestones.

Once a customer demonstrates meaningful and sustained utilization of its contracted capacity,
that capacity should be fully protected and remain available for the duration of the service
agreement, unless otherwise terminated under standard contractual provisions. These standards
should also recognize that under normal operating conditions sustained utilization may be less
than the maximum contracted capacity or phased energization rate. 1

This clarification is necessary to ensure that customers who fund and rely on transmission
capacity are not exposed to reallocation risk during development or after achieving operational
use.

Redline Recommendation
       (h) Non-utilized capacity.

        (1)     Not later than 30 days after a large load customer facility fails, by 6 months 3 years,

                to satisfy more than 80% of a milestone in its schedule for phased energization, the

                interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting TSP must notify ERCOT of the large

                load customer’s non-utilized capacity.




1
 Similar to other critical infrastructure or equipment, data center contract capacity should reflect the
maximum capacity required by engineered limits. A more familiar analogy is commercial aircraft design.
While commercial aircraft typically cruise under routine loads, they are engineered to safely withstand far
greater stresses from turbulence, maneuvering forces, and adverse conditions that may occur only
occasionally. Data centers, like aircraft and highway systems, are not sized only for average conditions—they
are designed for the highest conditions they may reasonably need to endure.
        (2)    Delays to the phased energization schedule may be allowed by the interconnecting

              DSP or interconnecting TSP as long as the large load customer demonstrates good

              faith efforts to satisfy the milestones in its schedule for phased energization or

              provides notice of force majeure and a revised schedule for phased energization.


       (f) Interconnection agreement.

       (10)          A new or existing large load customer that has satisfied all financial and

              energization obligations under its interconnection agreement shall retain its full

              contracted capacity and shall not be subject to any reallocation of capacity.


Conclusion:

STACK appreciates the opportunity to provide these comments and welcomes the opportunity to
work with Commission staff to refine these provisions to protect opportunities for continued
investment in Texas.



                                             Respectfully Submitted,



                                                    Kevin Hughes

                                                    Chief External Affairs Officer

                                                    Public Affairs

                                                    STACK Americas

                                                    khughes@stackinfra.com
      EXECUTIVE SUMMARY FOR STACK INFRASTRUCTURE COMMENTS TO
            PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION IN PROJECT NO. 58481




STACK Infrastructure (“STACK”) supports the Commission’s effort to establish a clear
framework for large load interconnection. STACK provides additional recommendations focused
on the treatment of non-utilized capacity under §25.194(h).

STACK supports financial commitments to ensure that transmission infrastructure costs are not
shifted to other ratepayers. However, as drafted, the proposed rule introduces uncertainty by
allowing for the reallocation of contracted transmission capacity. This creates risk for large-scale
investments that depend on long-term certainty of access to transmission service.

STACK recommends:

   •   Replace rigid timing triggers with utilization-based standards
       Contracted transmission capacity should not be subject to reallocation except in cases of
       clear and sustained non-performance. This ensures that capacity remains reserved for
       projects making meaningful progress towards energization and achievement of a capacity
       threshold, while avoiding unnecessary uncertainty for viable developments.
   •   Allow flexibility for delays outside customer control
       The rule should provide a reasonable cure period where delays are caused by factors
       outside the customer’s control, including force majeure events, transmission development
       timelines, or supply chain constraints.
   •   Protect contracted capacity after demonstrated use
       Once a facility achieves 80% of its contracted capacity, the full contracted capacity
       should no longer be subject to reallocation risk and should remain available for the
       duration of the service agreement, absent termination or material breach. This
       clarification is necessary to prevent utilities from reallocating capacity after substantial
       investment and demonstrated utilization.
